newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government reaches partial tax agreement.
newsitem.headline: German government reaches partial tax agreement.

text.p: The German government and the main opposition party reached a partial compromise on Monday on several key issues for changes in the 1997 tax code, but failed again to agree on key corporate tax cuts.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said late on Monday that the two sides had agreed to set aside unresolvable differences on the 1997 tax bill, which means that an existing "wealth tax" on financial and property assets would disappear in 1997.

Hamburg Mayor Henning Voscherau, who led the opposition Social Democrats in the tense discussions, claimed a victory over the centre-right coalition because child support money would be raised by 20 marks ($13.06) to 220 marks per month and child next year.
That had been a key demand of the SPD, whose leadership in the states gives it a majority in the upper house of parliament and an effective veto over the tax bill.
But Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners were also able to claim a partial victory -- the elimination of the wealth tax.
Officials of the two parties pledged to continue discussions on reforming corporate taxes, although they conceded time was running short.
The states will lose about nine billion marks in revenues throught the elimination of the wealth tax.

The partial agreement makes it unlikely the two sides will agree this year to eliminate the corporate assets tax, which the government says is necessary to keep the country attractive for capital investment.
The states are opposed because the revenues flow mainly to them.
The government has proposed raising the states' share of value-added tax as a compensation, but the states are not satisfied with the offer. ($1=1.5309 Mark)
